newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thai baht adjustment inevitable, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thai baht adjustment inevitable, analysts say.

text.p: Reform of the Thai currency system is inevitable after this week's stinging speculator attacks on the baht, analysts said on Thursday.
But they ruled out devaluation as a way of appeasing currency predators, saying it was likely to result in more grief than joy for the government and economy.
"The fixed exchanged rate, capital mobility and effective monetary policy cannot coexist," said an analyst from a U.S. brokerage firm.

"It is not the question of whether the Bank of Thailand has enough resources to defend the currency. I'm sure it does. But why allow the inflexible baht to be a constant irritation to the monetary policy?"

Analysts said Thailand could not afford to allow interest rates to come down in order to boost the sagging economy -- projected by private analysts to grow at a decade-low of less than six percent this year -- without letting go of the baht.
Most analysts declined to speculate on a time frame for any adjustment but some felt it could happen in six to 12 months.

Offshore speculators attacked the baht this week despite its high-yielding rates, forcing the currency to swing widely out of the four-satang band within which the Bank of Thailand now allows it to fluctuate.
The attacks forced the central bank to intervene heavily in the market along with other regional central banks and issue repeated denials of a devaluation or any currency adjustment.

The baht is now pegged to a basket of currencies, which is confidential, but believed to heavily weight the dollar. The dollar's weight was increased to about 80 percent in 1986 when it was clear that the dollar was trending down at a rapid pace, economists said.
The basket peg was suitable for Thailand during 1985-1995 as a long decline in the dollar kept the baht undervalued and Thai exports competitive, analysts said.
The system also made the baht one of the most stable currencies in the region and an easy target for interest rate arbitraging.
But the peg also attracted speculative attacks on the baht when the dollar jumped in February, resulting in considerable disruption in the domestic money market.
The Bank of Thailand has kept interest rates high to defend the baht against attacks, but this week its strategy came under pressure again as more attacks set in.
"If you allowed the baht to reflect market sentiment by making it more flexible, then you don't have to worry about interest rates," said Song Seng Wun of ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Singapore.

The Bank of Thailand intervened heavily to support the baht and pushed up the implied overnight interbank rate to punish speculators. The action did calm the market somewhat on Thursday as the baht was quoted at 25.790-25.890 against 26.330-26.430 late on Wednesday.
"There's blood on the streets. The speculators are being burned," said the head of trading at a European bank of the central bank action.
Chia Woon Khien, regional economist of Singapore-based Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken, speculated that the Bank of Thailand was likely to adjust the basket of currencies first.
The central bank could do so by gradually reducing the weight of the strengthening dollar in the basket and widening the trading band later when economic conditions stabilised.

"Between a re-balancing of the currency basket and a widening of the trading band, the (central bank) is likely to adopt the former first, given that the first is more discretionary and reversible," she said.
But the timing for any such adjustment was crucial, said Supavud Saicheua of Phatra Reseach.

A belief that the dollar was on the rise, concern about poor Thai export prospects and a still large current account deficit would be compelling reasons for people to believe that a more flexible baht could result in a weaker baht, he added.
"But we believe that a more flexible baht need not imply short-term disruption or induce damaging speculation if appropriately timed," he said in a report.
